summary: Proposes HighSpeed TCP, a change to TCP's congestion control for connections with large congestion windows. Standard TCP struggles to fill very fast, long paths. The RFC is experimental and notes that it is not a consensus that this is the best method for high-speed congestion control.

plainLanguage.summary: HighSpeed TCP changes how quickly TCP increases and reduces its sending window when the window is large. It keeps Standard TCP behavior at windows of 38 segments or less, but accepts less fairness with Standard TCP at lower loss rates.

subtitle: An experimental change to TCP congestion control for connections with large congestion windows.

tldr.problem: Standard TCP needs extremely rare congestion events to sustain very large windows on fast, long-delay paths. The RFC gives a 10 Gbps example requiring an average window of 83,333 segments.
tldr.mechanism: HighSpeed TCP behaves like Standard TCP up to a congestion window of 38 segments. Above that, it adjusts the increase and decrease after congestion using values derived from a response function and lookup table.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3649 is Experimental and explicitly says it does not represent consensus that this is the best high-speed congestion-control method. The RFC calls for experimentation and feedback.

today: RFC 3649 is Experimental and does not represent consensus that this is the best method for high-speed congestion control. The RFC invites experimentation and operational feedback.

sections.title: The Large-Window Problem
sections.content:
Standard TCP's average congestion window falls as packet loss increases. On a high-bandwidth path with a long round-trip time, filling the path can require a very large window and an unusually low loss rate. The RFC gives an example of 10 Gbps with 1500-byte packets and a 100-millisecond round-trip time, requiring an average window of 83,333 segments.

HighSpeed TCP changes TCP's response to congestion for connections with large windows. The RFC does not aim to change how connections start with large initial windows.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard TCP can need a very large sending window to use a fast path with a long round-trip time. HighSpeed TCP changes congestion control when that window becomes large.

sections.title: Design Goals and Limits
sections.content:
The design aims to improve throughput without requiring unrealistically low loss rates. It also aims to work without extra feedback from routers or receivers and to remain compatible with TCP in moderate or high congestion, such as packet drop rates of 1 percent or higher.

The RFC does not aim to preserve TCP-compatible performance at very low drop rates, to increase the window faster than slow-start allows, or to avoid oscillations in every one-way flow scenario. These are explicit limits of the proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: The change targets large windows and should not add load in moderate or heavy congestion. It does not promise the same share as Standard TCP at very low loss rates.

sections.title: How the Window Changes
sections.content:
HighSpeed TCP uses the Standard TCP response function at congestion windows up to Low_Window, set to 38 segments. Its upper design point is High_Window of 83,000 segments at High_P of 10^-7. Between these points, the RFC defines a response function for choosing congestion-control parameters.

In the absence of congestion, the window grows by a value based on a(w). After a congestion event, it decreases by a fraction based on b(w). At the upper design point, the RFC sets the decrease value to 0.1 and derives an increase of 72 segments per round-trip time.
sections.plainLanguage: At small windows, HighSpeed TCP follows the same rules as Standard TCP. At larger windows, it grows by larger amounts and reduces the window by a table-selected fraction after congestion.

sections.title: Fairness and Queueing Trade-Offs
sections.content:
At the same packet drop rate, HighSpeed TCP can obtain a larger congestion window than Standard TCP. The RFC's comparison gives relative fairness of 1.0 at drop rates of 10^-2 and 10^-3, 2.2 at 10^-4, and 10.2 at 10^-6. The authors say this trade-off needs feedback and further investigation.

Larger increases can also cause more packets to be dropped together in a Drop-Tail queue. At a window of 83,000 packets, the RFC says the increase is 70 packets per round-trip time, placing greater demands on router queue management.
sections.plainLanguage: HighSpeed TCP can take more bandwidth than Standard TCP when packet loss is low. Its larger sending increases can also put more pressure on router queues.

sections.title: Deployment and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says HighSpeed TCP behaves exactly like Standard TCP whenever the congestion window is less than 38 segments. Its effect also depends on the receiver's advertised window being large enough to permit a large congestion window. The proposal needs no changes to routers or receivers.

The Security Considerations section says the proposal does not change TCP's underlying security. The RFC is experimental and says it does not establish consensus that this is the best method for high-speed congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: HighSpeed TCP changes only connections whose sending window grows beyond the stated threshold. The RFC is an experiment, not a consensus choice for high-speed congestion control.

references.text: Allman, M., Paxson, V., and W. Stevens, "TCP Congestion Control", RFC 2581, April 1999.
Handley, M., Floyd, S., Padhye, J., and J. Widmer, "TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC): Protocol Specification", RFC 3448, January 2003.
